name: Otoplasty (ear pinning)

card.summary: Surgery that sets protruding ears closer to the head; a long-established procedure with high reported satisfaction, usually discussed in looksmaxxing as a cheap add-on.
card.note: Evidence is mostly surgical case series and reviews; over 200 techniques exist and overcorrection or suture problems are documented.

quick.overview:
Otoplasty reshapes or repositions the cartilage of the outer ear. For prominent ears it is usually done by creating or restoring the fold of the antihelix, reducing a deep conchal bowl, or repositioning a protruding lobe. The aim is to bring the ear closer to the head.

In looksmaxxing forums it is often described as a high-return, relatively low-cost add-on, and some members say prominent ears can undermine otherwise balanced facial features. Reviews in the surgical literature describe high patient satisfaction, but note that no single technique is considered definitive.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons either use stitches that bend the cartilage into a fold without cutting it, score or cut the cartilage so it bends back, or remove a portion of the conchal cartilage. Some centres also describe closed, needle-based or minimally invasive versions. A head band is typically worn for several weeks afterwards to protect the shape.
quick.risks: Documented complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, scarring, recurrence of prominence and overcorrection with an unnatural contour. A large case review of 562 patients reported significant morbidity including residual deformity. Forum members also discuss revision surgery for lobe or helix irregularities. Surgery is an Rx medical procedure performed by licensed surgeons.

lead: Otoplasty, commonly called ear pinning, is plastic surgery of the outer ear (auricle). It is most often performed to correct prominent ears, sometimes called "bat ears" or "elf ears" in forum slang, which result from an underdeveloped antihelical fold, an enlarged conchal bowl, or a protruding earlobe. [1][2] The same family of operations is also used for congenital malformations such as constricted ears, Stahl's deformity and cryptotia, and for ear reconstruction. [3][4]

For appearance, the goal is to bring the ears closer to the head so that they sit in proportion with the rest of the face and no longer draw the eye from the front or in profile. A German review describes protruding ears as affecting about 5 percent of the population and as a minor anatomical variant that can nonetheless cause real emotional distress, particularly through teasing in childhood. [23] Reviews report good to very good cosmetic results with standard techniques. [23]

Surgical reviews describe prominent ears as the most common abnormality of the external ear, and note that more than 200 different techniques have been described. [5][6] One 2005 review concluded there is no clearly definitive technique, while another noted that despite the variety patient satisfaction is generally high. [3][5] Evidence for otoplasty consists mainly of case series, retrospective comparisons and expert reviews, alongside a handful of randomized comparisons of technique. [20][21]

In looksmaxxing communities otoplasty is discussed as a small but visible surgical add-on, frequently mentioned alongside jaw surgery and rhinoplasty. [7] Members debate its payoff, its ideal timing and the risk of ending up with ears that look "pinned". [8][9] A newer thread of research looks at ear position as part of overall facial attractiveness, including injectable approaches that push the auricle outward rather than back. [27]

paras: The auricle is a cartilage framework covered by thin skin. Prominence typically arises from a missing or shallow antihelical fold, an overly deep concha, a protruding lobule, or a combination. [1][10] Beyond prominent ears, otoplasty techniques are used for constricted ears, Stahl's deformity, cryptotia and macrotia. [3][4]

Reviews note that the physical consequences of prominent ears are minor, while the aesthetic and psychological effects can be substantial. [3] Naumann's 2008 review describes affected children as facing teasing, with reported low self-esteem, social withdrawal and school difficulties in some cases, and notes that children may downplay their distress even when parents see it. [23]

The American Society of Plastic Surgeons describes ear surgery as changing the shape, position or proportion of the ears, covering protruding ears, overly large ears (macrotia), injury-related deformities and earlier ear surgery that left the patient dissatisfied. It lists healthy, non-smoking teens and adults with specific goals, and children from about age five, as typical candidates. [31]

Surgical approaches are commonly grouped into those that keep the cartilage intact and use sutures to create a fold, those that score or cut the cartilage so it bends, and those that remove cartilage to reduce projection. [10] Named methods include Mustarde mattress sutures, Furnas conchamastoid sutures, Stenstrom anterior scoring, and the closed Merck stitch method. [10]

Naumann's review links technique to cartilage quality: Mustarde sutures suit soft, thin cartilage typical in children, while incision-and-scoring methods (Stenstrom, Chongchet, Crikelair) or cartilage thinning are described for stiffer cartilage; Furnas cavum rotation addresses a large concha and lobulopexy addresses a protruding lobule. [23] One review describes mattress sutures to create an antihelical fold as offering benefits that outweigh their risks, and conservative resection of the concha for prominent conchal bowls; it also states that a surgeon should be comfortable with several techniques. [2] A 1968 paper laid out the aesthetic goals for correcting protruding ears, and a postauricular fascial flap has been described as an adjunct to Mustarde and Furnas-type repairs to reduce relapse. [24][26]

Surgeon opinion papers describe differing preferences between cartilage-cutting and cartilage-sparing approaches. [11] Authors of a 2022 BMC Surgery paper describe a performance-optimized otoplasty workflow aimed at efficiency. [28]

Minimally invasive and closed techniques have also been reported, including a German series of 385 ears corrected by a closed technique building on a 1967 method by Kaye, and later reviews of minimally invasive otoplasty. [12][13] Naumann notes that long-term data on minimally invasive variants were limited at the time of his review. [23] An implantable clip system has been evaluated in a pilot study. [14]

Wikipedia notes that surgery for prominent ears may be carried out from about age four to six, once the ear is close to adult size, and that general anesthesia is often used in children. [10] Naumann reports that most ear growth in width is complete by about age six and in length by about 11 to 12, and that otoplasty does not significantly affect later growth. [23] A Grokipedia summary reports surgery typically around ages 4 to 6. [15]

Adults can also be treated, often under local anesthesia. [23] Community posts note that some surgeons are reluctant to operate on teenagers because of scarring concerns, a claim made by forum members rather than established in the reviewed literature. [9]

In newborns, non-surgical ear molding with tape or splints is described as feasible during the first weeks of life while cartilage remains pliable. [10] Naumann reports poorer molding results when started after about three days of life. [23]

A bulky dressing is typically worn for several days, followed by a snug headband worn at night for roughly three to six weeks. Swelling and bruising usually subside within about two weeks, and the final shape may take longer to settle. [10] A registered trial of 70 participants compared postoperative bandage protocols in otoplasty. [29]

sections.h: Effects on appearance and quality of life
paras: A study of 62 children and adults treated with suture techniques reported improved health-related quality of life and patient benefit. [19] Reviews describe satisfaction as generally high across techniques. [5][25] Authors of a 2018 review of cosmetic otoplasty describe the operation as rewarding but exacting, requiring attention to anthropometric norms. [1]
A registered study planned to enrol about 1,500 people is examining the impact of plastic and aesthetic surgery on self-esteem. [30]

In the broader literature on facial attractiveness, a 2025 randomized study examined an injectable technique behind the ear that lateralizes the auricle and reported on its pan-facial effects in Chinese patients. That approach moves the ears outward rather than pinning them back, showing that ear position is being studied as one element of overall facial perception. [27]

A literature review of complication rates found that over 200 techniques exist but relatively few articles report complication rates; early complications included hematoma and infection. [16] A review of 562 consecutive cases reported significant morbidity, including residual deformity, hemorrhage, infection, keloid or hypertrophic scarring and anterior skin necrosis. [17]

Wikipedia lists hematoma, infection (including perichondritis), suture extrusion, skin necrosis from tight dressings, and overcorrection with unnatural contour. [10] Naumann lists suture granuloma (up to about 4 percent with non-absorbable sutures), keloids, hypertrophic scars and recurrence as later complications and suggests photographic follow-up at 6 and 12 months. [23] Surgical authors have suggested that technical errors, rather than springy cartilage, account for many failed primary procedures. [2]

On looksmax.org, members describe concerns such as outward-turned lobes, a downward-pointing upper helix and extra folds after pinning, and discuss revision otoplasty. [8] These are personal accounts, not systematic data.

Human studies of otoplasty are largely case series and surgical comparisons. A randomized comparison of rasps versus puncture needles for creating an antihelical fold has been published, as has a study comparing a standard and a modified Chong-Chet technique with long-term follow-up. [20][21]

A controlled study examined ear sensibility after otoplasty, and a study of 62 children and adults using suture techniques reported improvements in health-related quality of life and patient benefit. [22][19] A German series of 385 ears corrected with a closed technique reported on a large number of patients. [12] A 2016 pilot study evaluated an implantable clip system. [14] A 1991 critical review in The Laryngoscope assessed published clinical results. [25]

A review of 562 consecutive cases documented complication rates including residual deformity needing revision. [17] No large randomized trial has compared otoplasty with no surgery for appearance outcomes in adults seeking facial improvement.

Among looksmaxxing forum users, otoplasty is described as an inexpensive add-on compared with jaw surgery; one poster called it a "high roi" option, while another replied that neither rhinoplasty nor otoplasty was important. [7] One thread claims it can boost facial masculinity more than custom implants, which is a community opinion that has not been tested. [8]
A 2019 study of Google search interest in facial cosmetic procedures is among the public-interest analyses that include ear surgery. [18]

Related options discussed alongside otoplasty include earlobe repair or reduction, revision otoplasty after overcorrection, infant ear molding, and injectable or implant approaches that change ear projection. [8][10][27] Community members also discuss pairing otoplasty with jaw surgery and rhinoplasty in one planning cycle. [7]

timeline.event: Ear surgery is described in the Sushruta Samhita, an ancient Indian medical text. [10]
Johann Friedrich Dieffenbach reports a surgical approach for prominent ears. [10]
Edward Talbott Ely performs an ear pinback procedure in New York City. [10]
Mustarde describes a suture-based technique and Stenstrom describes anterior cartilage abrasion. [10]
Kaye publishes a closed approach later revisited in minimally invasive otoplasty. [12]
A review of 562 consecutive otoplasty cases documents morbidity including residual deformity. [17]
Naumann publishes a review of otoplasty techniques and risks. [23]
A literature review of otoplasty complications is published in JPRAS. [16]
A pilot study evaluates an implantable clip system for prominent ears. [14]
A randomized trial compares rasps and puncture needles for antihelical fold creation. [21]
A randomized study examines postauricular injection to lateralize the auricle and its effect on facial attractiveness. [27]

lore.intro: Otoplasty appears on looksmax.org as an add-on to jaw surgery or as a standalone fix for prominent ears. [7][8]

claims.claim: Otoplasty is a "high roi" add-on to jaw surgery
claims.believers: Posters planning bimaxillary surgery ask whether to add it and some say it is the more worthwhile of the minor procedures. [7]
claims.experts: No published study ranks otoplasty against other appearance procedures; reviews report high patient satisfaction and quality-of-life gains in case series. [5][19]

claims.claim: Pinning ears back can raise facial masculinity more than custom implants
claims.believers: A forum thread asserts it is life-changing for people with prominent ears. [8]
claims.experts: No studies compare otoplasty with facial implants for perceived masculinity. A study of 62 patients reports improved health-related quality of life after suture otoplasty. [19]

claims.claim: Otoplasty can leave deformities such as outward lobes or downward upper helix
claims.believers: Posters describe these outcomes and propose revision surgery or heavy earrings. [8]
claims.experts: Reviews list overcorrection, residual deformity and recurrence among documented complications. [10][16][17]

claims.claim: Teenagers are poor candidates because of scarring
claims.believers: A forum reply says surgeons are hesitant at 12 to 18 because of hypertrophic scar risk. [9]
claims.experts: The reviewed literature on techniques does not give an age-specific rule in the sources consulted; keloid and hypertrophic scarring are listed as complications. [17]

claims.claim: Ear position matters for overall facial harmony, not just the ears themselves
claims.believers: Forum posters pair otoplasty with jaw surgery on the view that prominent ears undermine an otherwise balanced face. [7][8]
claims.experts: Reviews describe aesthetic and psychological effects of prominent ears as substantial despite minor physical consequences, and a 2025 study examined auricle position and facial attractiveness. [3][27]

claims.claim: Revision surgery can correct problems from a first otoplasty
claims.believers: Posters describe lobe procedures and revision otoplasty as routes to fix outward lobes or extra folds. [8]
claims.experts: Reviews note that residual deformity and recurrence occur and that revision cases have been analysed. [16][17]

claims.claim: Otoplasty is a minor procedure with short downtime
claims.believers: Posters describe it as cheap and quick compared with jaw surgery. [7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes surgery of about 1.5 to 5 hours with a headband worn for 3 to 6 weeks and swelling settling in about two weeks. [10]
